articles.title: Storing users' API keys in a Windows desktop app with DPAPI, from Python, without a dependency
articles.excerpt: A bring-your-own-key desktop app ends up holding a lot of other people's secrets. Ours stores keys for speech recognition, translation and LLM providers in a JSON settings file under the user's profil…
articles.body: A bring-your-own-key desktop app ends up holding a lot of other people's secrets. Ours stores keys for speech recognition, translation and LLM providers in a JSON settings file under the user's profile. For the first versions they sat there in plain text. Anything that could read the user's files could read the keys: backup tools, sync clients, a careless "send me your settings file" over support chat. On Windows the standard answer is DPAPI. CryptProtectData encrypts bytes with a key derived from the current user's logon credentials. Only the same user on the same machine can decrypt them with CryptUnprotectData . There's no key file to manage and no password prompt. This post covers how we wired it in with plain ctypes and, more importantly, how the migration and failure paths work.

articles.title: Search Results That Jump Back to an Old Query in React: Finding and Fixing the Race
articles.excerpt: The problem A developer built a search bar in React. Each time the user types a letter, the component sends a request to the server and shows the results. Most of the time it works. But sometimes the…
articles.body: The problem A developer built a search bar in React. Each time the user types a letter, the component sends a request to the server and shows the results. Most of the time it works. But sometimes the list shows results for an older, shorter search. The box says "react", and the list shows results for "r". Typing slowly hides the bug. Typing fast makes it show up again. This is a common bug, and it is easy to miss in local testing, because a local server answers almost every request at the same speed. The root cause Every keystroke starts a new request. The network does not promise that answers come back in the same order the requests went out. A short query like "r" can match many rows and take longer on the server. A longer query like "react" can come back fast.

articles.title: Why AI Agent Cache Hit Rates Collapse: GPT, Claude, and Auditable Gateways
articles.excerpt: A source-backed guide to third-party agent cache failures, GPT and Claude prompt-caching mechanics, reproducible hit-rate measurement, and Modelflare's public compensation boundary. AI agent caching i…
articles.body: A source-backed guide to third-party agent cache failures, GPT and Claude prompt-caching mechanics, reproducible hit-rate measurement, and Modelflare's public compensation boundary. AI agent caching is not a checkbox. It is a protocol, routing, and accounting contract. This article explains why an opaque third-party agent can show a very low cache hit rate even when the upstream model supports prompt caching, how GPT and Claude measure reuse differently, and what an auditable gateway should guarantee. The decision in one sentence Do not put a production, cache-sensitive agent behind a third-party agent or gateway that cannot expose native cache usage, preserve a stable prefix, keep model and route affinity, and reconcile the result against a durable ledger.

articles.title: A 1.5% redirect rate looked fine. One site's sitemap was 92% redirects.
articles.excerpt: I probed 1,089 sitemap URLs across 119 sites with redirects switched off. 1,062 came back 200. Sixteen came back 301. That is a 1.5% redirect rate, which reads like a rounding error — the kind of numb…
articles.body: I probed 1,089 sitemap URLs across 119 sites with redirects switched off. 1,062 came back 200 . Sixteen came back 301 . That is a 1.5% redirect rate, which reads like a rounding error — the kind of number you put in a slide and move on from. Then I grouped the same results by domain. Two sites accounted for all sixteen: one at 11 of 12 (92%) , one at 5 of 12 (42%) . The other 117 sites contributed zero. The aggregate number was not a measurement of the fleet. It was 1,062 green lights diluting two red ones. That is the bug this post is about, and it is not a redirect bug. The redirects were correct and intentional. The bug was that my sitemap validator — and probably yours — had been reporting on an XML file for months and calling it a verdict on the server.

articles.title: What Graphium can do 03: Calculate between cells of a table
articles.excerpt: When you write down a bread recipe, you often want the hydration: the weight of the water divided by the weight of the flour. A Graphium note has a calculation block that works things out as you type,…
articles.body: When you write down a bread recipe, you often want the hydration: the weight of the water divided by the weight of the flour. A Graphium note has a calculation block that works things out as you type, with variables and units. Write cell("table", "row", "column") there, and it reads one cell from a table in the same note, so you can calculate between cells. water = cell("Dough", "Water", "Weight") flour = cell("Dough", "Flour", "Weight") water / flour * 100 The row is found by the name written in the table's first column. You can also point at a row by its number, but then adding or reordering rows makes the line read a different value, and the line doesn't tell you which value it used.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 28, 1971: Britain launches its 1st satellite Prospero into space on a Black Arrow rocket
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 28, 1971, the United Kingdom launched its first satellite. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 28, 1971, the United Kingdom launched its first satellite. The satellite was named Prospero, but it was also known as the X-3. This wasn't Britain's first satellite , but it was the first and only one the British space program launched with one of its own rockets. The first six British satellites all launched from the United States on NASA rockets. Prospero launched on a carrier rocket called the Black Arrow. The Prospero mission was the fourth and final flight of a Black Arrow rocket . Prospero was designed to study how the environment in space affects communications satellites. It tested things solar cells and telemetry systems, and even had a micrometeoroid detector that would determine small particles in space posed a threat to the spacecraft.

articles.title: 5 days beneath the waves: What it's like to live in an underwater 'space station'
articles.excerpt: Confined inside a research station 22 feet (7 meters) underwater, Analog Astronaut Commander Dr. Musilova and her crew performed research and maintenance activities like future astronauts on Mars.
articles.body: Living underwater was surprisingly peaceful. It was in many ways exactly what I imagine living on Mars would be like one day. There were no humans around us, except for my three SEA STAR crewmembers and me. Apart from the human noises we made, we couldn't hear anything other than the life support systems keeping us alive submerged 22 feet (7 meters) below the surface. We were living in these extreme conditions to study the challenges astronauts may face on long-duration space missions. Since performing research in space is still rare and expensive, there are numerous facilities around the world that focus on recreating space-like conditions on Earth . One of those stations is the Jules' Undersea Lab, where the SEA STAR simulated space mission took place.

articles.title: ISS astronaut will conduct Canada's 1st spacewalk in 7 years on Oct. 29: Watch it live
articles.excerpt: Joshua Kutryk will venture outside the International Space Station on Oct. 29, on the first spacewalk by a Canadian astronaut in more than seven years. Here's how to watch it live.
articles.body: The next International Space Station (ISS) spacewalk will have more maple-leaf flavor than usual, as a Canadian astronaut will become the first to go outside the orbiting complex in seven years. Canadian Space Agency (CSA) astronaut Joshua Kutryk, who's also a colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force, will help the ISS boost its power supply during his first-ever spacewalk on Thursday (Oct. 29). Kutryk will be joined by NASA astronaut Anil Menon, who has done three spacewalks already and also serves as a colonel with the U.S. Space Force . The duo are scheduled to venture outside the orbiting lab at 8 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT), kicking off a spacewalk that will last roughly 6 hours and 45 minutes. You can watch it live here at Space.com , courtesy of NASA, beginning at 6:30 a.m. EDT (1030 GMT).

articles.title: Meet Apeiron, Virgin Galactic's 1st 'Delta-class' space plane
articles.excerpt: Virgin Galactic has officially unveiled its first "Delta-class" space plane, and announced the results of the worldwide vote to choose its name.
articles.body: Virgin Galactic has officially unveiled the first space plane in its next-gen "Delta" line, and announced the results of the worldwide vote to choose its name. Spaceship Apeiron will be the first Delta-class vehicle, Virgin Galactic revealed on Wednesday (Oct. 28). Apeiron (pronounced "A'-per-on," according to the announcement) takes its name from the ancient Greek word meaning "boundless," and was selected through a public poll that drew votes from thousands of people across 83 countries and six continents. The reveal comes on the same day that the space plane is scheduled to be flown from its manufacturing facility in Mesa, Arizona, to Spaceport America in New Mexico, where the vehicle will undergo final preparations before beginning flight tests.
